meta.title: Ukrainian B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Ukrainian → English (see the Ukrainian, recall the meaning) and English → Ukrainian (see an English meaning, recall the Ukrainian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise whilst travelling, to produce simple connected text on topics which are familiar or of personal interest, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Ukraine certifies proficiency in the language but publishes no graded word list, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 391 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and a career, education and learning, the media and technology, the environment, society and politics, law and crime, money and banking, health and a way of life, relationships and feelings, culture and the arts, the problems of travel, giving an opinion and arguing it, describing people and things, and the verbs of deciding, changing, comparing and making — and the other 609 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Ukrainian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Cyrillic with its stress marked (кни́га, роблю́), because Ukrainian stress can fall on any syllable and move as the word changes, and nothing else shows it; there is no transliteration, and the Ukrainian Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters. The 481 nouns show their gender, their genitive and their plural; the 322 verbs show their aspect, imperfective or perfective, with the other verb of the pair beside them, their я and він forms and their past; and behind the All forms fold every noun's seven cases and every verb's tenses by person. Real example sentences come with 973 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 924 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, aspect, stress and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
